questiontext.text:
Conjecture: for all positive real numbers \(a\) and \(b\), \(\ln(ab)=(\ln a)(\ln b)\).

Give a counterexample. Type e for the number \(\mathrm{e}\), and e^2 for \(\mathrm{e}^2\).

\(a=\) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] \(b=\) [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]]

generalfeedback.text:
A counterexample is a pair of positive numbers \(a\), \(b\) for which \(\ln(ab)\neq(\ln a)(\ln b)\). Choose values whose natural logarithms you know exactly.

Take \(a=b=\mathrm{e}\). Then \(\ln(ab)=\ln(\mathrm{e}^2)=2\), but \((\ln a)(\ln b)=1\times 1=1\). Since \(2\neq 1\), the conjecture is false.

The correct law of logarithms is \(\ln(ab)=\ln a+\ln b\): the logarithm turns a product into a sum, not into a product.

The conjecture is true for some pairs. Writing \(u=\ln a\) and \(v=\ln b\), it says \(u+v=uv\), that is \((u-1)(v-1)=1\). So \(a=b=1\) (where \(u=v=0\)) and \(a=b=\mathrm{e}^2\) (where \(u=v=2\)) both satisfy it, which is why the first values you try may not work.

questionnote.text: Fixed: Exercise 7, a positive pair with ln(ab) not equal to ln(a)ln(b) (e.g. a = b = e).

questiondescription.text: This question is directly adapted from Exercise 7 in Section 3 (p. 8) of Bokhove, C., Thoma, A., Gammack, D., Yu, L. H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022.

falsefeedback.text: The conjecture is only about positive \(a\) and \(b\) (\(\ln\) is not defined for \(0\) or negative numbers), so a counterexample must use positive values.

falsefeedback.text: For your values both sides equal {@L7@}, so the conjecture is true for this pair. (Both \(a=b=1\) and \(a=b=\mathrm{e}^2\) are such pairs.) Try other values.
